title: Myasthenic crisis following iodinated contrast material (iohexol) aspiration: a case report
case_prompt:
A 48-year-old Sinhalese man with a 2-year history of acetylcholine receptor–positive myasthenia gravis presented for an upper gastrointestinal contrast study to evaluate 3 months of progressive dysphagia to solids and then liquids. He underwent thymectomy in 2016 and had two prior myasthenic crises precipitated by respiratory infections, both requiring mechanical ventilation. His maintenance medications included pyridostigmine 50 mg every 6 hours, mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily, and daily prednisolone; he was functionally independent with 5/5 limb power and normal respiratory parameters on admission.

Under fluoroscopic guidance, 10 mL of iohexol was administered orally, but the contrast entered his right main bronchus, and the study was aborted. He was transferred to the emergency unit on high-flow oxygen with SpO₂ above 90%, but 45 minutes later his respiratory rate fell to 10 breaths per minute and his work of breathing declined. Nebulized salbutamol and a single 500 mg dose of IV metronidazole were given without improvement, and he required endotracheal intubation using IV midazolam and atracurium. A chest radiograph showed only right apical segment collapse. He was then transferred to the intensive care unit with a working diagnosis of respiratory distress due to contrast aspiration.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Aspiration pneumonitis was the initial working diagnosis — “According to the clinical scenario, the diagnosis of respiratory distress due to contrast aspiration was made…”  
2. Myasthenic crisis was diagnosed after neurologic reassessment given worsening neuromuscular weakness — “he was then evaluated by a neurologist and the diagnosis was revised to myasthenic crisis, possibly due to aspiration pneumonitis caused by aspiration of contrast.”  
3. Guillain–Barré syndrome was considered but rapid onset of symptoms made it unlikely — “rapid onset of symptoms … made them remote possibilities.”  
4. Cholinergic crisis was considered but absence of excess cholinergic symptoms like small pupils or bradycardia made it unlikely — “absence of excess cholinergic symptoms like small pupils or bradycardia … made them remote possibilities.”  
5. Electrolyte imbalance was considered but normal electrolytes made it unlikely — “normal electrolytes … made them remote possibilities.”
